subject: language_arts

unit.title: Apostrophes & homophones
unit.essentialQuestion: When does a word need an apostrophe, and how do I pick between sound-alike words?

title: The apostrophe trap: NOT for plurals
objectives: By the end, I can tell a plural (no apostrophe) from possession/contraction (apostrophe).

vocabulary.definition: two words squashed into one — apostrophe marks the missing letters
it's = it is (squash); its = belonging to it (no apostrophe)
vocabulary.example: It's raining. The dog wagged its tail.

emphasize: Apostrophes are NEVER for plain plurals — two cats, never cat's.
The one diagnostic question: is something BELONGING, or are letters MISSING? If neither, it's just a plural — no apostrophe.
The its/it's test: say 'it is' — if it fits, it's; if not, its.

keyConcepts: apostrophes only for contraction or possession
misconceptions: the greengrocer's apostrophe — adding one to any word ending in s (banana's for sale, two car's)
it's/its backwards — assuming belonging always needs an apostrophe
over-correcting and stripping apostrophes from real possessives/contractions
hooks: Be the sign inspector — shops get this wrong all the time; badge on, catch the fake apostrophes!

digital: wrong-sign cards on screen (apple's 50p, two car's, fresh egg's)

plan.goal: The apple's 50p sign — spot that nothing belongs and nothing is missing, so the apostrophe is a mistake; retrieve both jobs.
plan.note: The sign-inspector frame carries the lesson. Cross out the wrong apostrophe with a flourish.
plan.successCriteria: Child recalls the two jobs (squashing, belonging) and agrees the sign apostrophe is fake.

script.say: I saw a sign at a shop. It said apple's 50p. Hmm… is that right? Do the apples OWN anything? No! Nothing's belonging, no letters missing — so that apostrophe is a MISTAKE. Today you're the sign inspector, catching apostrophes that shouldn't be there. Badge on — let's inspect! Quick kit-check first: when DO we use an apostrophe? You've learned two jobs.
script.adaptHints: Listen for: squashing words (contraction) and belonging (possession). If shaky, quick re-show: don't (squash) and Sam's bag (belonging) — 'only those two times.'

elements.value: nothing belongs, nothing missing — no apostrophe!

stuckProtocol: If the two jobs won't come: show don't and Sam's bag side by side — 'squash… belonging… those are the ONLY two apostrophe jobs.'

plan.goal: Teach the big rule (never for plurals) and the one diagnostic question; introduce the its/it's test.
plan.note: Two-column contrast is the core visual: two cats vs the cat's tail. Then it's raining vs its tail.
plan.successCriteria: Child can say the question: is something belonging, or are letters missing? If neither — no apostrophe.

script.say: Big rule: an apostrophe is NEVER for a plain plural. Two cats — more than one cat — no apostrophe! But the cat's tail — belonging — DOES get one. So I ask one question: is something BELONGING, or are letters MISSING? If neither, it's just a plural — leave the apostrophe out. And a special pair: it's with an apostrophe means it is — test by saying 'it is'. Its with NO apostrophe means belonging to it. The dog wagged its tail — say 'it is tail'? No! So no apostrophe.
script.adaptHints: Chant the question rhythmically: 'belonging? missing letters? neither — no apostrophe!' Keep the its/it's test to one clean demo.

rows: yes — the tail belongs to the cat
belonging word its — special, like his/her
blocks.caption: Plurals NEVER take an apostrophe. Only belonging or missing letters do.

plan.goal: Shared inspections: fix two car's and fresh egg's, then sort a mixed set into contraction / possession / plural.
plan.note: Ask the diagnostic question aloud for every item before the child sorts it.
plan.successCriteria: Child sorts the six items correctly, asking the question aloud.

script.say: Inspect this sign with me: two car's. Is anything belonging? Are letters missing? No — it just means more than one car. So we cross that apostrophe out: cars. Now fresh egg's — same check — eggs! Right, inspector: here's a whole crate of phrases. Sort each one into its pile: squashed words, belonging, or plain plural. Ask the question out loud every time.
script.adaptHints: If the child rushes, slow them with the two-part question before each drag. Celebrate each caught fake with inspector flair.

blocks.prompt: Sign inspector: sort each phrase into the right pile.

check.question: Is two dogs written dog's or dogs?
check.expectedAnswer: dogs — no apostrophe, it's just a plural

wrongAnswers.why: greengrocer's apostrophe — adding one near any s
wrongAnswers.remedy: Ask the question: do the dogs own anything? Are letters missing? No and no — so…?

wrongAnswers.why: half-remembered rule about apostrophes after s
wrongAnswers.remedy: That's a mark for another year! Today: plain plural, more than one — what does a plain plural get? Nothing at all.

plan.goal: The lesson's diagnostic: true or false — two dogs is written dog's.
plan.note: This exact item is in the End-of-Unit 3 check. 'True' = the greengrocer misconception.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers False and explains: nothing belongs, no letters missing — just a plural.

script.say: Inspector's exam question. True or false: two dogs is written d-o-g-apostrophe-s, dog's.
script.adaptHints: After a correct answer, probe: 'How do you know it's not belonging?' — listen for 'the dogs don't own anything; it just means more than one.'

blocks.explain: False! Nothing belongs and no letters are missing — it's a plain plural: dogs. Plurals never take an apostrophe.

check.question: True or false: two dogs is written dog's.

wrongAnswers.why: over-applied the apostrophe near s — the greengrocer's apostrophe
wrongAnswers.remedy: Do the dogs OWN anything? Are letters missing? No — just more than one. Plurals get no apostrophe.

wrongAnswers.answer: False, because it should be dogs'
wrongAnswers.why: swapped one wrong apostrophe for another
wrongAnswers.remedy: No apostrophe anywhere! Run the question: belonging? missing letters? Neither — so the s stands alone: dogs.

plan.goal: Independent inspecting: apostrophe-or-not decisions on mixed plurals, possessives and contractions; its/it's for fast finishers.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. The question must be asked aloud before every decision — it is the habit.
plan.successCriteria: Child decides correctly on 4+ of 6 mixed phrases, leaving plurals bare and keeping real apostrophes.

script.say: Full inspector duty! I'll show you signs and sentences — some apostrophes are real, some are fakes, and some words are missing the apostrophe they need. Ask our question out loud each time: belonging? missing letters? Then decide.
script.adaptHints: Theme the fake signs around shops the child knows (bakery, sweet shop, pet shop). Never change the target words.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'let's ask our one question.'
Step down: use the yes/no gate — 'Is something belonging?' then 'Are letters missing?'
ONE hint: 'if you answered no to both, it's just a plural.'
Keep it safe: 'Even shops get this wrong — that's why we inspect carefully.'

plan.goal: Child states the inspector's rule; end on a win.
plan.successCriteria: Child says: a word with s gets NO apostrophe when it's just a plural; apostrophes only for belonging or missing letters.

script.say: Tell me the rule a sign inspector lives by — when does a word with s NOT get an apostrophe? … Exactly: when it's just a plural, more than one. Apostrophes only for belonging or missing letters. You caught the fake apostrophes and kept the real ones — a sharp-eyed sign inspector. You even cracked its and it's.
script.adaptHints: Praise the observed process: asking the question before deciding. Tease Lesson 14: 'next, three words that SOUND identical — the ones grown-ups muddle most.'

block.statement: A plain plural like three cats never needs an apostrophe.
block.explain: True — plurals just mean more than one. Apostrophes are only for belonging or missing letters.

wrongAnswers.why: still attaching apostrophes to any s
wrongAnswers.remedy: Run the question on three cats: belonging? missing letters? No and no — so what does the s get? Nothing!

wrongAnswers.why: invented a sub-rule
wrongAnswers.remedy: No exceptions for animals, fruit or anything else — a plain plural NEVER takes an apostrophe.

hints: What are the only two apostrophe jobs?
Does 'more than one' match either job?

reteach.say: The apostrophe has exactly two jobs — squashing and belonging. 'More than one' isn't a job! Three cats, two dogs, ten sweets — the s stands alone every time.

block.caption: three cats — no apostrophe, just more cats

block.prompt: Fix the shop sign: banana's for sale
options: banana's for sale is already right
block.explain: The bananas don't own anything and no letters are missing — plain plural, no apostrophe: bananas for sale.

wrongAnswers.answer: banana's for sale is already right
wrongAnswers.why: the greengrocer's apostrophe looks normal from seeing it on real signs
wrongAnswers.remedy: Ask the inspector question: do the bananas OWN anything? Are letters missing? Neither — so the apostrophe is a fake.

wrongAnswers.why: moved the apostrophe instead of removing it
wrongAnswers.remedy: It doesn't need an apostrophe ANYWHERE — it's just more than one banana. Cross it right out.

hints: Neither — so the apostrophe must go.

reteach.say: Shops write banana's, apple's, egg's — and they're all wrong! It's just MORE THAN ONE. Inspector's fix: cross the apostrophe out and let the s stand alone: bananas for sale.

practiceBank.skill: sort contraction vs possession vs plural

block.prompt: Sort each phrase into the right pile.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: I'm hungry + she'll win → contraction; the dog's bone + Gran's hat → possession; two buses + five sweets → plural

wrongAnswers.why: any s-ending word pulled towards the apostrophe piles
wrongAnswers.remedy: Do the buses own anything? Are letters missing? No — 'more than one' has its own pile.

wrongAnswers.why: saw the apostrophe and defaulted to squashing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Try the stretch test: 'the dog is bone'? Nonsense! So it's not a squash — who owns the bone?

hints: Ask the question for each: belonging? missing letters? neither?
Stretch test for squashes: can you say 'is' or the two long words?

reteach.say: Three piles, one question. I'm hungry — I am — letters missing: squash pile. Gran's hat — Gran owns it: belonging pile. Two buses — just more than one: plural pile, no apostrophe. Question first, pile second.

wrongAnswers.why: assumed belonging always needs an apostrophe
wrongAnswers.remedy: Use the test — say 'it is': 'the dog wagged it is tail'? No! So no apostrophe: its.

wrongAnswers.why: invented an apostrophe-after-s form
wrongAnswers.remedy: its is a special belonging word like his and her — it never takes an apostrophe at all.

hints: Say 'it is' in the gap — does it make sense?
No 'it is'? Then it's the belonging word: its.

reteach.say: The its/it's test never fails: say 'it is'. 'The dog wagged it is tail' — nonsense! So we want the belonging word its, no apostrophe. its belongs to the family of his and her — none of them take apostrophes.

wrongAnswers.why: over-corrected after learning its — dropped a needed apostrophe
wrongAnswers.remedy: Say the test: 'it is raining outside' — it fits! Letters are missing, so we need the squash: it's.

wrongAnswers.why: apostrophe drifted to the end
wrongAnswers.remedy: The squash of it is puts the apostrophe where the i of is dropped: it's.

hints: 'It is raining' works — so which spelling shows the squash?

reteach.say: Same test, other way round: 'it is raining' makes perfect sense — so this one IS the squash, and squashes need their gravestone: it's raining. Test first, spelling second.

block.statement: In 'the cat's tail', the apostrophe is correct, because the tail belongs to the cat.
block.explain: True — belonging is one of the apostrophe's two real jobs. Inspectors remove fakes but protect the real ones!

wrongAnswers.why: over-correcting — now stripping ALL apostrophes near s
wrongAnswers.remedy: Careful, inspector — don't arrest the innocent! Ask the question: does the tail belong to the cat? Yes — so this apostrophe is real.

wrongAnswers.answer: True, because cat's means many cats
wrongAnswers.why: right answer, plural reasoning
wrongAnswers.remedy: cat's with an apostrophe is ONE cat who owns something. Many cats would be plain cats — no apostrophe.

hints: The tail belongs to the cat — which job is that?

reteach.say: A good inspector does two things: removes fake apostrophes AND protects real ones. The cat's tail — belonging — real, keep it! Two car's — nothing belongs — fake, cross it out. The question tells you which is which.

options: Three banana's sat in the bowl.
block.explain: Only the first shows belonging — the skin belongs to the melon. The others are plain plurals wearing fake apostrophes.

wrongAnswers.why: counted apostrophes as decoration for plurals
wrongAnswers.remedy: Two melons — do they own anything in that sentence? No — plain plural, no apostrophe.

wrongAnswers.why: the greengrocer's apostrophe again
wrongAnswers.remedy: Run the question on the apples: belonging? missing letters? Neither — cross it out.

hints: Only one sentence has real belonging in it.
Whose skin is it? That's your clue.

reteach.say: Tricky — all four LOOK similar! The secret: hunt for real belonging. The melon's skin — the skin belongs to the melon — real apostrophe. Everywhere else it's just counting fruit, and counting never needs an apostrophe.

rows: yes — the melon owns its skin

block.prompt: Be the sign writer! Write one CORRECT shop sign with a plural in it — like Fresh buns 20p.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: A sign with a plural spelled with no apostrophe (e.g. Fresh buns 20p)

wrongAnswers.why: the fake apostrophe sneaks back in the child's own writing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Inspect your own sign! Do the buns own anything? Are letters missing? Then the s stands alone.

wrongAnswers.why: dodging the risk instead of applying the rule
wrongAnswers.remedy: Be brave — you know the rule! Pick something the shop sells lots of, and let the plain s do its job.

hints: Pick something a shop sells lots of.
More than one = plain s, no apostrophe.

reteach.say: Sign writers keep it simple: name the things (plural, plain s), add the price. Fresh buns 20p. Juicy plums 50p. No apostrophes anywhere — nothing belongs, nothing's missing. Write yours and then inspect it like a pro.

block.prompt: The bird flapped ___ wings. AND ___ going to rain. Which pair fills both gaps?
block.explain: 'it is wings' fails → its (belonging). 'It is going to rain' works → It's (squash).

wrongAnswers.why: the test applied backwards
wrongAnswers.remedy: Say 'it is' in each gap. 'Flapped it is wings'? No → its. 'It is going to rain'? Yes → it's.

wrongAnswers.why: belonging always given an apostrophe
wrongAnswers.remedy: its is the special belonging word — no apostrophe ever. Which gap is about the bird OWNING its wings?

hints: Run the 'say it is' test on each gap separately.
Belonging → its. A real 'it is' → it's.

reteach.say: Double test time. Gap one: 'the bird flapped it is wings' — nonsense, so belonging: its. Gap two: 'it is going to rain' — perfect sense, so the squash: it's. One test, asked twice, gets both.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave sign-fixing with its/it's items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the yes/no gate spoken aloud (belonging? missing letters?), then a level-1 item.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 4+ correct across levels 2–3 including one categorize sort, one fixed plural sign and one its/it's item → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'apostrophe vs plural'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'let's ask our one question.'
Step down: yes/no gate — 'Is something belonging?' then 'Are letters missing?'
ONE hint: 'no to both? Then it's just a plural.'
Keep it safe: 'Even shops get this wrong — that's why we inspect carefully.'
adaptivity.personalization: Set the wrong signs in shops the learner loves (sweet shop, pet shop, toy shop) and use their pets/family for the real possessives. The spoken question stays in every framing.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a catchable fake sign; praise the process — 'you asked the question before every decision, like a real inspector.'

differentiation.support: Use the single yes/no gate 'Is something belonging?' as the only decision; sort just plurals vs possessives (drop contractions and its/it's).
differentiation.stretch: Fix its/it's in two sentences and explain the test; spot a real greengrocer's apostrophe on an actual shop sign or leaflet and correct it.

extension: Design one correct shop sign and one deliberately wrong one, then explain the difference like an inspector's report.
assessmentEvidence: Child correctly leaves plurals apostrophe-free and keeps apostrophes for possession/contraction in at least four of six phrases, and states 'plurals never take an apostrophe'.
revisitLater: End-of-Unit 3 check asks the child to mark two dogs as dogs. Bring back the its/it's test as retrieval before Lesson 14; the categorize sort returns in Lesson 15's review bank.
